system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 21 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

PROCEDURE NAME:  Exchange with a tunneled hemodialysis catheter.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with end-stage renal disease and non-maturing
right upper extremity AV fistula.  Exchange of left temporary HD catheter with
a tunneled hemodialysis catheter was requested.

RADIOLOGISTS:  This procedure was performed by Dr. ___ Dr. ___,
the attending radiologist, who was present and supervising throughout the
entire procedure.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  After explaining the risks and benefits of the
procedure, informed written informed consent was obtained from the patient.
The patient was placed supine on the angiographic table and the patient's left
neck and chest were prepped and draped in standard sterile fashion.  A
preprocedure timeout was performed.

After injection of 1% lidocaine at the left upper chest and exit site of
indwelling temporary HD catheter, an incision was made at the exit site of the
tunneled hemodialysis catheter.  A 15.5 ___ tunneled hemodialysis catheter
with 23 cm tip-to-cuff length was placed through the subcutaneous tunnel into
the neck incision site.  An Amplatz guidewire was advanced through the
indwelling temporary HD catheter into the IVC under fluoroscopic guidance and
indwelling temporary HD catheter was removed.
A ___ ___ tip sheath was advanced over the wire into the SVC and using a ___
kumpe catheter and 0.0.35 glide guide wire, access was gained into the right
subclavian vein and a venogram was obtained, which demonstrated widely patent
central veins with small collateral veins at the level of th eproximal
subclavain vein. Sheath and catheter were removed and a peel- away sheath was
advanced into the SVC under fluoroscopic guidance. The guidewire and inner
portion were removed and a tunneled hemodialysis catheter was placed through
the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned at the right atrium.  A final
chest x- ray demonstrated proper location of the tip at the right atrium.

The neck incision was closed with #4 Vicryl sutures and the catheter was
secured to the skin with 0 Prolene sutures.  The catheter was flushed,
heplocked, and a sterile dressing was applied.  The patient tolerated the
procedure well and there were no immediate complications.  Moderate sedation
was provided by administering divided doses of 50 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of
Versed throughout the total intra-service time of 30 minutes during which the
patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored.

length and tip positioned at the right atrium.  The catheter is ready for use.

right subclavain vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the emergency room because your blood pressure dropped very low and you were bleeding from a wound on your right thigh. We’ve put pressure on it and given you some blood. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel weak… and dizzy. The wound’s been oozing for days, but today it just gushed. I didn’t know what to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your blood count was very low, and your blood was too thin from the Coumadin you’re on. We’ve given you blood, vitamin K, and stopped the Coumadin for now. You’ll be going to the ICU for close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay? I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in good hands. We’re stabilizing you now. You’ve had several units of blood, and your pressure is improving. We’ll keep a close eye on you overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your hemoglobin is slowly improving. We’re continuing to monitor your wound. The blood culture from last night is still pending, but we started antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics? Is there an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. Because of your kidney disease and the wound, we want to be cautious. We’ll know more in a day or two. For now, you’re on vancomycin and ceftazidime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had your first dialysis session. We removed some extra fluid because you were overloaded. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. My breathing feels easier. But my leg still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The wound care team looked at your thigh. It’s not infected, but it’s deep. They recommend continuing the special dressing. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood culture came back. It grew a type of bacteria called viridans streptococcus. It’s likely from your mouth or skin, but we’re treating it with antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I don’t have any sores in my mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can get into the blood through small breaks. Since you have kidney disease and a wound, we’re being extra careful. We’ll continue the vancomycin and watch for any fever or changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your legs to check for blood clots. Good news — no clots were found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve had clots before, so I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and because of that history, we’ll restart blood thinners once the bleeding risk is lower. For now, we’re focusing on healing the wound and treating the bacteria in your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are negative — that’s great. It means the antibiotics are working and the infection wasn’t widespread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your blood pressure is stable, your hemoglobin is up to 10.1, and you’re not bleeding anymore. We’re planning to move you to the regular floor today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan to make sure there’s no abscess or other source of infection. Everything looks clear — no abscess, no pneumonia, no belly issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my heart? Could the bacteria have gone there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echocardiogram. No sign of infection on your heart valves. Your heart function is normal. So we’re confident this was a brief bloodstream infection, not endocarditis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to replace your dialysis catheter. The old one was pulled out a bit and not working well. We’ll put in a new tunneled one under X-ray guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’ve had infections from lines before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s routine. We’ll use sterile technique and give antibiotics. We’ll also check your veins with a venogram to make sure there’s no narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. New catheter is in place, and your veins are open. There’s a small collateral vein, but no blockage. You can resume dialysis tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel safer knowing my access is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 7.7 when you came in — very high. Now it’s coming down. We’ll restart Coumadin at a lower dose once we’re sure you’re not at risk for more bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on it for my clots. Should I be worried about them coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart it soon, at 5 mg daily. You’ll need frequent INR checks at the nursing home. Goal is around 2 to 3. We’ll also give you heparin shots until it kicks in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a debridement of the wound — just cleaned out some dead tissue to help it heal. No surgery needed. The wound care team will keep managing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels a little sore. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, some soreness is expected. We’ll keep the pain meds going. The dressing helps it heal from the inside out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has been well controlled on your insulin. Keep up the good work with your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on a soft diet because I have no dentures. I sometimes feel food gets stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange for dentures at the nursing home. If you still have trouble swallowing after that, we may need a swallowing study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your hemoglobin is stable at 32.1%. You’ve stopped needing blood. Your kidney function is as expected for your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. When can I go to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. You’ll need dialysis three times a week, wound care, and INR monitoring. Once we confirm everything’s set up, you can transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried an MRI to check if the infection reached the bone, but you moved too much. A later scan showed no osteomyelitis. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was uncomfortable lying still. I’m glad it’s not in the bone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the CT of your legs showed no calciphylaxis. Just vascular calcification, which is common with kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.0 — perfect. We’ve started Coumadin at 5 mg daily. Keep the heparin shots until your next check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure the nurses check it every few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The final blood cultures are negative. You’ve completed a week of vancomycin and will finish a two-week course. We’ll give it during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the bacteria is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. We’re finishing the course to be sure. The strain was sensitive to vancomycin, so treatment worked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is healing. The itching you feel is a good sign — new skin is forming. Keep using the papain-urea ointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It itches a lot. Can I use something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you diphenhydramine for itching. Avoid scratching — keep the dressing on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged your transfer to the extended care facility. They’ll continue your dialysis, wound care, and INR checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. I just want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your daughter will be contacted. She’s your main contact. We’ll send all instructions to the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s out of town, but she’ll come when she can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. Last day of IV vancomycin tomorrow. After that, just Coumadin and wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m grateful for all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your labs are stable, wound is clean, no fever. You’re ready for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have chest pain, leg swelling, bleeding, or fever. Keep up with dialysis and wound care. And get those dentures!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pack your things — you’re leaving tomorrow morning. We’ll send all meds and instructions to the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep following up, and take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Time to go. You’re stable, and the facility is ready for you. We’ll check in with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything. I’m ready for the next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Stay strong, and keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll miss the nurses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll miss you too. You were a great patient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best sign of all. Keep that hope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, and a history of DVT, was admitted from a skilled nursing facility for hypotension and significant bleeding from a right thigh wound. Her INR was critically elevated at 7.7 due to warfarin therapy, contributing to hemorrhagic shock. She received multiple blood transfusions, vitamin K, and reversal agents. During her ICU stay, she was aggressively ultrafiltered due to volume overload. Blood cultures revealed viridans streptococci, prompting a two-week course of vancomycin, though repeat cultures were negative and imaging ruled out endocarditis or abscess. A tunneled dialysis catheter was placed after removal of a malfunctioning line, with venography showing patent central veins. Wound care was optimized, and anticoagulation was restarted with warfarin, bridged with heparin. She stabilized, transitioned to the medical floor, and was discharged to extended care with plans for ongoing dialysis, wound management, and INR monitoring.
